issues.description: Re-ingest upserts new rows but never removes rows or aliases that disappeared from the input tree, so reports can include stale data.
Format B assumes metrics is a dict; a truthy non-dict metrics value raises AttributeError and aborts ingestion instead of producing a warning.
Format C parses XML with ElementTree without catching ParseError, so one malformed XML file aborts the entire ingest.
Format A accepts non-finite score strings such as nan, which later cause SQLite integrity failures or invalid score handling.
Format B accepts JSON NaN/non-finite numeric scores through json.loads and numeric type checks, leading to database failures or invalid values.
Format C accepts non-finite score text such as nan because float() is unchecked before clamping and insertion.
clamp_score does not reject NaN, so invalid scores bypass range checks because all comparisons are false.
Format A does not validate required run_id, model, or task fields, allowing blank keys and empty canonical data.
Format B converts missing/null ids and fields with str(), allowing values like 'None' or empty model/task names into canonical rows.
Format C allows missing ids, model names, and tasks, which can collapse unrelated runs under the same unique key.
Format C never validates that the XML root is results, so structurally wrong documents with run children are ingested as valid.
XML parsing uses the standard ElementTree parser directly, which is a poor default for untrusted XML because malicious XML can create denial-of-service risk.
The CLI calls ingest before checking for zero discovered files, so an empty input directory still creates or mutates a database before returning an error.
Format A reads the entire CSV file into memory and parses by splitlines, which is fragile for large files and quoted multiline CSV fields.
Format B reads the entire JSONL file into memory instead of streaming line by line.
Ingest accumulates every parsed record and warning before writing, increasing memory use instead of streaming through the transaction.
Report builds per-model score lists in Python rather than using SQLite aggregates, which can become slow and memory-heavy on large result tables.
